source.title_on_document: Experimental Evidence on the Learning Impact of Generative AI

supplement.where: Hyperlinked 'Supplementary Materials' (p. 1 footnote; p. 6, Section 2; p. 7 fn. 4; p. 12); no URL printed in the text. Appendices A-C (pp. 51-93) are in this PDF.
supplement.holds: Survey instruments, full text of the reading materials, and the essay grading instrument. No statistics for the similarity or quality outcomes are said to sit there; all estimates used here are in Tables 5, 6, and A5 of this PDF.

paper_design_summary: In a two-session lab experiment at Middlebury College (Spring 2025), undergraduates were randomly assigned to an AI-allowed condition (logged-in ChatGPT GPT-4o account, any generative AI permitted) or an AI-forbidden condition while they learned an unfamiliar topic and wrote an analytical essay of about 500 words. About one week later all students wrote a second essay on a complementary prompt without AI or other resources. Essays were scored by Prolific graders and an LLM grader for quality, and by sentence embeddings for within-group similarity (homogenization) and similarity to the reading.

studies.label: Two-session lab RCT: AI-allowed vs AI-forbidden analytical essay writing (Session One with AI, Session Two unaided one week later)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Access to generative AI (AI-allowed with a logged-in ChatGPT GPT-4o account vs AI-forbidden) during the 35-minute learning and essay-writing phase of Session One. In each of eight time slots one of two parallel labs was randomly assigned to each condition, and each student signed up for the slot was randomly assigned to a computer in one of the two labs.
assignment.quote: The first session employs a between-subjects design with random assignment to either an AI-allowed or AI-forbidden condition.
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 2.1 (Overview); strata = eight Session One time slots, p. 11, Section 3.3

arms.name: AI-allowed
arms.description: Instructions permit any generative AI tool; browser tabs open to a dedicated logged-in ChatGPT (GPT-4o) account, Wikipedia, and the Middlebury College Library website; standard online resources also allowed (pp. 8, 52).

arms.name: AI-forbidden
arms.description: Instructions prohibit generative AI tools; browser tabs open to Google, Wikipedia, and the Middlebury College Library website; standard online resources allowed (pp. 8, 52).

participants.exclusions: Table 2 (p. 36) reports treatment assignment for all 256 students who completed the sign-up survey (126 AI-forbidden, 130 AI-allowed). 211 attended Session One (104 control per Table 3/4 N; 107 AI-allowed per Table A1 N); 45 assigned students did not attend (82.5 vs 82.3 percent attendance, p. 11). 204 attended both sessions (Table 4 Session Two N = 204, control 102). Essay similarity samples: Session One N = 210 (control 104) in Table 5, but N = 209 for the same rows in Table A5; Session Two N = 199 (control 99). The paper does not state why one Session One essay and five Session Two essays drop from the similarity regressions. Arm n_analyzed above are Session One attendees; AI-allowed counts are 211 - 104 and are printed directly only in Table A1 (N = 107).
participants.who: Undergraduates at Middlebury College recruited campus-wide for 'a study on learning' (AI not mentioned); mean age 20.1, mean GPA 3.68, 35.1 percent male among Session One attendees.
participants.quote: the 256 students who completed the sign-up survey (column 1), the 211 (82.4 percent) who attended Session One (column 2), and the 204 (79.7 percent) who attended both sessions (column 3).
participants.locator: p. 10, Section 3.2; p. 35, Table 1; p. 36, Table 2

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT (GPT-4o), dedicated logged-in account provided by the researchers; any generative AI tool permitted
ai_tool.how_used: Free use during the 35-minute learning phase in which students read and wrote the Session One essay. Logs show 67.3 pp take-up of the provided account; uses included explaining concepts (57 percent of treated students in logs), drafting responses, summarizing, editing (pp. 14, 29). No AI in Session Two.

task.description: Analytical essay (about 500 words) on an assigned technical topic (blockchain, carbon capture, or CRISPR) answering a prompt that asks students to analyze relationships between concepts and support the analysis with evidence; two prompts per topic, one randomly assigned to each session (pp. 7, 69-71). Not a creative task; it falls under the codebook's clause for writing tasks compared across writers for similarity.
task.duration: Session One: up to 35 minutes for learning and writing combined; Session Two: 20-minute essay, about one week later (pp. 7, 9)

outcomes.name: Within-group similarity of Session One essays (written with AI available to the treatment arm)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Average pairwise cosine similarity between a student's essay embedding and all other essays in the same treatment x topic x prompt cell; sentence-embedding model fine-tuned from MPNet. Higher = more homogeneous (sign is reversed relative to the codebook's diversity direction). Also shown in SD units in Figure 6 and Figure A5 (figure only) and repeated in Table A5 Panel D.

contrasts.reported: Within-group sim.: control mean 0.774; ITT 0.001 (SE 0.007); TOT 0.001 (SE 0.010); N = 210 (control 104). Text: 'a 0.1 percent change relative to the control mean of 0.774', statistically insignificant. Table A5 Panel D repeats 0.774, 0.001 (0.007), 0.001 (0.010) with N = 209.
contrasts.locator: p. 39, Table 5 Panel C, columns 1-3; p. 17, Section 4.3; p. 65, Table A5 Panel D

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity of each essay to all other essays in its treatment x topic x prompt cell (higher = more similar)
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Sentence-embedding model (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) fine-tuned from the MPNet architecture (Song et al., 2020); exact checkpoint not named
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each essay against all other essays in the same treatment x topic x prompt cell (within-arm pools split by topic and prompt)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: OLS of the student-level similarity score on treatment with strata fixed effects and double-lasso controls; heteroskedasticity-robust SEs (scores share a pool within each cell but are treated as independent); TOT by 2SLS
diversity_detail.notes: Validation (p. 13 fn. 11): within-topic similarity 0.74 vs 0.15 across topics; same prompt 0.78 vs same topic different prompt 0.71. AI-allowed arm includes students who did not use AI (67.3 pp take-up); ITT is the effect of access.

outcomes.name: Within-group similarity of Session Two essays (written unaided about one week later)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same measure as S1-O1, computed on Session Two essays written by all students without AI or other resources on the complementary prompt. Higher = more homogeneous.
outcomes.delay: About one week; mean 6.99 days between sessions, 61.4 percent exactly seven days (p. 9 fn. 5)

contrasts.reported: Within-group sim.: control mean 0.762; ITT -0.005 (SE 0.013); TOT -0.007 (SE 0.019); N = 199 (control 99).
contrasts.locator: p. 39, Table 5 Panel C, columns 4-6; p. 65, Table A5 Panel D

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity of each essay to all other essays in its treatment x topic x prompt cell (higher = more similar)
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Sentence-embedding model (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) fine-tuned from the MPNet architecture (Song et al., 2020); exact checkpoint not named
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each essay against all other essays in the same treatment x topic x prompt cell
diversity_detail.uncertainty: OLS on student-level scores with strata fixed effects and double-lasso controls; heteroskedasticity-robust SEs; TOT by 2SLS
diversity_detail.notes: The text discusses the Session One similarity result only; the Session Two similarity estimate appears in Table 5, Table A5, and Figures 6 and A5.

outcomes.name: Overall essay quality, Session One (with AI available to the treatment arm)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Holistic 0-10 overall quality rating, averaged across 3-4 Prolific graders (master's or PhD holders, blind to condition) and an LLM grader (Claude Opus 4.8) using the same rubric. Rubric judges accuracy, evidence, relevance, structure, and style, not creativity, so coded question 'none' (see notes). Variants: quality index (mean of five dimensions), the five dimensions, and human-only and AI-only scores (Table A6, Figure A4).

contrasts.reported: Overall quality (average): control mean 6.190; ITT 0.246 (SE 0.211); TOT 0.373 (SE 0.321); N = 209 (control 104). Text: 0.25 points 'or 0.17 SD, p = 0.245'. Quality index: control mean 6.450; ITT 0.190 (0.183).
contrasts.locator: p. 40, Table 6 Panel B, columns 1-3; pp. 17-18, Section 4.3

outcomes.name: Overall essay quality, Session Two (written unaided about one week later)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Same grading as S1-O3 on Session Two essays. Coded question 'none' because the rubric rates analytical quality, not creativity; by the codebook's mechanical rule (AI removed) it would be after_ai. Significant dimension effects: writing style 0.411 (0.169), relevance 0.409 (0.198).
outcomes.delay: About one week; mean 6.99 days (p. 9 fn. 5)

contrasts.reported: Overall quality (average): control mean 5.076; ITT 0.308 (SE 0.210); TOT 0.459 (SE 0.317); N = 197 (control 97). Text: 0.31 points 'or 0.20 SD', p = 0.143. Quality index: control mean 5.297; ITT 0.281 (0.183).
contrasts.locator: p. 40, Table 6 Panel B, columns 4-6; p. 21, Section 5.2

eligibility.reason: Students were randomly assigned to generative-AI access vs no AI (p. 6) for an essay-writing task whose outputs are compared across writers by embedding similarity (p. 13; Table 5 Panel C, p. 39), the codebook's across_people clause. People analyzed: 210 for Session One similarity, 199 for Session Two, out of 211 Session One attendees and 256 randomized. Eligibility rests on the similarity outcomes only: the task is an analytical essay, and its quality ratings do not measure creativity.

one_line_finding: AI access did not change how similar students' essays were to each other: within-group cosine similarity ITT 0.001 (SE 0.007) on a control mean of 0.774 with AI in Session One, and -0.005 (SE 0.013) on 0.762 in unaided Session Two essays one week later (p. 39, Table 5 Panel C).
open_questions: Does an analytical essay on a technical topic belong in the creativity section only through its across_people similarity outcome? I coded the quality outcomes as question 'none'; Review 1 may prefer with_ai/after_ai with construct 'usefulness'.
Session One similarity N is 210 in Table 5 but 209 in Table A5 for identical estimates; the paper does not explain the one-essay difference or why Session Two drops to 199 from 204 attendees.
Similarity is computed within treatment x topic x prompt cells, so each arm's essays split across three topics x two prompts; the student-level regression SE treats these scores as independent.
The atlas owner (Reyes) is a coauthor; a conflict-of-interest note may be needed on the site.
notes: Outcomes left out of the list: test scores (learning, not creativity), self-assessed knowledge, AI-detected fraction and plagiarism (Table 5 Panel A), length, readability, and lexical diversity indices (Table 5 Panel B; lexical diversity is within one essay, not across people), similarity to the reading material (Table 5 Panel C; one essay vs the source text, not across people; S1 ITT -0.004 (0.009) on 0.746, S2 0.001 (0.013) on 0.704), the five quality dimensions as separate outcomes, and heterogeneity by automation vs augmentation users (Table 8, quality and test scores only). No similarity heterogeneity is reported. The paper names no preregistration. Printed page numbers match PDF page numbers.
